newsitem.title: MEXICO: FEATURE - Mexico president now taking harder line.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Mexico president now taking harder line.

text.p: He won office, a shy technocrat promising grand reforms to end more than 60 years of one-party rule in one of the world's fastest-growing countries.
But in his third year, opposition politicians and analysts say Mexican President Ernesto Zedillo has changed.

The timid, hesitant economist who presided over a disastrous peso devaluation in his third week of office and saw his support evaporate has given way to an aggressive, confident politician with rising popularity.
Recent opinion polls show that -- for the first time since Mexico's December 1994 economic crisis -- more than half of the population believe Zedillo is doing a good job.

Zedillo, 45, has stepped up tours of the provinces, pressing flesh, opening buildings and handing out land titles -- acting like a traditional Mexican leader rather than the promised reformist bent on reducing the office's huge powers.

The president and his aides deny a change of strategy, but independent analysts say the new Zedillo image is intended to help his Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) keep its Congressional majority in key July elections.

"Zedillo has become a political militant," left-wing commentator Miguel Angel Granados Chapa told Reuters. "The PRI has convinced him he needs to put the prestige of the presidency at the service of the party. Otherwise, he risks disaster in July."
UPSET AT BROKEN PROMISES

Electioneering by presidents is hardly unusual. But what has upset Mexicans tired of a 68-year-old regime is that Zedillo has not kept his promises to share power with the opposition, negotiate consensus reforms for greater democracy and stand above politics so that the PRI could lose an election if voters so desired.

Instead, critics say Zedillo has dismissed the only opposition cabinet member, rammed generous election funding for political parties through Congress despite opposition protests and sanctioned aggressive attacks on non-government parties.

"I think the hardliners basically came to Zedillo and said 'This reform is all very well, but we're losing elections, so stop it'," Felipe Calderon Hinojosa, president of the biggest opposition party, told Reuters.

Calderon's National Action Party (PAN) is still smarting from the humiliating ouster in December of its top official in the Zedillo government -- then Attorney General Antonio Lozano -- after allegations of incompetence.

The same month, Zedillo dismissed Santiago Onate, a concilatory negotiator, from the presidency of the PRI. His replacement was Humberto Roque Villanueva, a rough-and-tumble politician best known for an obscene gesture to send opponents on the floor of Congress the message: "We screwed you".
Roque has lived up to expectations, blasting the PAN as fascists and the left-wing Party of the Democratic Revolution (PRD) as thugs who betray their country "for a plate of lentils".
"POLITICS COME FIRST"

"Zedillo's agenda has effectively been stopped by PRI hardliners and by the opposition," said Federico Esteves, a political scientist at the ITAM university in Mexico City. "The technocrats' time is over -- politicians come first now."

Peace negotiations with Zapatista rebels in the southern state of Chiapas have stagnated since Zedillo backtracked on a government promise to grant Indians greater autonomy. Anti-government protesters complain of greater intolerance.

Gerardo Fernandez Norona, the leader of a debtors' group, said last week he and two colleagues were detained, locked up in a jail with common criminals for four days, and faced trumped-up charges simply because they tried to deliver a letter to Zedillo as he left a bankers' convention in the resort of Cancun.
Analysts say Zedillo's unexpected change of course was forced upon him by circumstance and political pressure.

"Zedillo was starting to feel very isolated," said political scientist Jose Antonio Crespo. "He had no alternative but to give in to pressure from the hardline groups and agree to ally himself with them."

His promise of a "healthy distance" from the PRI led to a dangerous gap opening up between party and president, the economic crisis hurt his popularity, and the opposition was not convinced that he was serious about change, Crespo added.
The main beneficiary within the PRI, political commentators say, has been the so-called Atlacomulco group, a hardline faction named after a town in the state of Mexico.
Among the leading lights of the Atlacomulco group is Carlos Hank Gonzalez, a former Mexico City mayor and minister who is commonly dubbed one of the party's most powerful old-guard "dinosaurs".

Hank appeared at a PRI convention last month to choose the party's candidate for mayor of Mexico City, waving to supporters as the delegates obligingly voted for "his" man, reporters who covered the event said. Asked about the acclaim, Hank smiled and said: "We dinosaurs have many friends".
